title: When the Internet Goes Down, Your Security System Should Not
description: Most organisations assume their security system will keep working when connectivity drops. In practice, many do not — because the system was installed without a fallback. With communicators like the Inner Range T4000 Pro now offering dual-SIM failover and VPN support built in, there is no longer a meaningful reason to leave your site vulnerable to a network outage. title: Your Physical Security System Is an IT Asset — Is Your IT Team Treating It That Way?

title: IQP Inspections for Access-Controlled Doors: The Compliance Check Most NZ Building Owners Overlook
description: Every access-controlled door in a New Zealand building with a compliance schedule carries a legal obligation under the Building Act — an annual inspection by an Independently Qualified Person, or IQP. The door must be inspected, tested, and reported to the local council each year, confirming it is performing to its specified standard. In practice, most building owners either do not know this applies to them, or they leave it until a compliance failure surfaces during a council audit. Red Wolf holds IQP qualifications and carries out these inspections as part of a broader access control service. We check that each door is latching, locking, and releasing correctly under all conditions — including alarm activation and power failure. If it is not performing to standard, we fix it and issue the required documentation. With the end of the calendar year approaching, now is a practical time to check whether your compliance schedule is current. If you are not sure whether your doors need an inspection, we can tell you in a short conversation what is required and what it will cost.

title: The NZ Minister for Police Just Briefed Security Leaders on Policy Changes — Here Is What It Signals for Businesses
description: The New Zealand Security Association recently shared news of an ASIS NZ Chapter event featuring Hon. Mark Mitchell, Minister for Police, Corrections, and Emergency Management. The session was focused on how recent legislative changes and national safety priorities should be informing the decisions of security executives, risk leaders, and operational managers right now. Ministerial-level engagement with the security industry is rare and it is worth taking seriously. It signals that the regulatory direction of travel in New Zealand is toward higher standards — particularly around the Protective Security Requirements framework, which sets expectations for how government-connected organisations and their supply chains manage physical security. For businesses operating in regulated sectors, or those supplying services to government, understanding how PSR obligations are evolving is no longer optional. It is part of how you demonstrate competence in a tender and how you manage liability when something goes wrong. Red Wolf works with clients in regulated environments and can help translate what these policy shifts mean for your security programme.

title: A New Study Found That Less Than Half of Organisations Are Confident in Their Active Assailant Response — Here Is What NZ Businesses Should Do About It
description: ASIS International and Everbridge released research this week showing that less than half of respondents are highly or mostly confident their staff know what to do in an active assailant incident. Four factors were linked to higher confidence: a comprehensive written plan, regular drills, communications technology, and a functioning behavioural threat assessment and management team. The gap between having a security system and having a prepared organisation is exactly what this finding describes. A camera at the front door and a monitored alarm panel do not tell your staff what to do when something happens. Physical security has two components — the technology layer and the human layer. Most businesses invest in the first and largely ignore the second. The organisations with the highest confidence in their readiness have both: documented procedures, tested regularly, supported by the right technology, and owned by someone with the authority to act. If your business has never run a scenario exercise or reviewed its emergency response documentation, that gap is worth closing before you need it.

title: It Is the Final Week of Security Awareness Month — One Check Every NZ Business Should Do Before November
description: October is Security Awareness Month, and this is the last week of it. Every year, this month creates a window where security conversations that normally get deferred actually happen. We want to use that window to ask one simple question: when did you last check whether the people responsible for your physical security actually know what the system does? Not the technical manual. The real-world question: if your alarm triggered at 2am on a Sunday, would the right person know who to call, what to do, and how to tell if the response worked? Physical security technology is only as effective as the people operating it. If your staff are not sure what system they have, who monitors it, or how to respond to an event, that is a gap worth closing this week — not next quarter.
